cf.title: pg_dump: skip pg_init_privs entries for non-existent roles

input.subject: BUG #19483: pg_upgrade fails with orphan records in pg_init_priv catalog table

verdict_reasoning: No objection survived at levels 1a or 1b: the patch fixes a reproducible pg_upgrade failure and follows the pg_dump direction suggested in message #4. Two fixable design points remain at level 2: standards-compat-1 (dropping an aclitem whose grantor alone is dangling causes lasting dump drift) and maintenance-fit-1 (no server version gate on the filter). Neither blocks the idea, but a committer who knows pg_dump's ACL code has to accept the trade-off and the backpatch range.

brief.title: pg_dump: skip pg_init_privs entries that name dropped roles
brief.problem: On servers before v17, DROP ROLE can leave pg_init_privs ACL entries that point to the dropped role by numeric OID. pg_dump emits these as GRANT or SET SESSION AUTHORIZATION "<oid>", so pg_upgrade from such clusters fails during restore after --check passed. The reporter hit this upgrading v14 to v18 with extensions installed by a role later dropped.
brief.proposed_design: pg_dump filters each initprivs array on the server and drops any aclitem whose grantor or grantee OID is missing from pg_roles, but keeps PUBLIC (grantee 0). It applies a SAFE_INITPRIVS macro in getAdditionalACLs(), which runs once per dump, and in the per-table column ACL query. An object whose items are all dangling gets no initial privileges.
user_visible_surface: pg_dump output: dangling-role aclitems from pg_init_privs no longer appear in GRANT, REVOKE or SET SESSION AUTHORIZATION.
After upgrade, affected extension members lose their pg_init_privs row, so later dumps re-emit the extension's own REVOKE and GRANT lines.
Separate proposal, HEAD only: aclitemout (putid()) would quote all-digit role names so they differ from dangling OIDs.
author_claims: A failed pg_upgrade becomes a restore that works, with two extra harmless lines in later dumps.
Overhead is about 1 to 2 ms on the one-time pg_init_privs fetch and does not grow with object count.
Laurenz Albe saw no noticeable effect in a pg_upgrade --link of 20000 empty tables.
pg_dump still works as a non-superuser because the check uses pg_roles instead of pg_authid.
The fix can be backpatched to v15; pg_upgrade uses the new cluster's pg_dump, so the v18 copy fixes the v14 to v18 case.
brief.thread_state: Laurenz Albe and Rui Zhao reviewed v9 and Rui reports no open items; the CF entry has gone back to Needs review after Waiting on Author. Tom Lane's objections about per-object query cost, and his putid() HEAD-only idea, got no visible final answer from him on v6 and later.
unclear: Whether Tom Lane accepts the v6 to v9 design, with the subquery running once per table in dumpTable().
Whether the putid() HEAD-only patch was written or submitted.
The CF target says version 19 but the patch also targets backpatch to v15; the final backpatch range is not agreed.
No test covers dumps from v15 or v16 source servers, where the problem actually occurs.

prior_attempts.title: pg_upgrade fails with non-standard ACL
prior_attempts.quote: I'm not generally enthusiastic about adding pg_upgrade code to predict whether the dump will fail to restore, because such code will never be as good as just trying the restore.
prior_attempts.reason: The author stopped responding after Noah Misch's March 2021 review, so the entry sat in Waiting on Author until Daniel Gustafsson returned it in November 2021. That review showed that the generated script still let the final pg_upgrade fail on a REVOKE ... FROM PUBLIC, and that the check compared obj_ident without obj_type. Noah Misch also had doubts about the approach, since pg_upgrade code that predicts restore failures cannot match a real restore.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P3 had pg_upgrade predict restore failures from ACLs and ask the user to run a cleanup script. This proposal dropped the pg_upgrade check from message #1 and makes pg_dump skip the dangling aclitems, so the restore itself succeeds.

objections.title: Dropping whole aclitems leaves upgraded extensions with permanent dump drift
objections.failure_scenario: A DBA upgrades a v15 cluster whose extension owner was dropped. The new cluster has no pg_init_privs row for those members, so every later pg_dump emits REVOKE and GRANT lines after CREATE EXTENSION. A restore against a newer extension version where a member was renamed then fails, and schema-diff tools report privilege changes nobody made.
objections.argument: The filter drops an aclitem when only its grantor is dangling, so a valid PUBLIC grant such as =r/16384 also leaves pg_init_privs (messages #33, #35). The patch now documents this drift, but documenting it does not remove it. A committer would likely ask why the patch drops these items instead of mapping the dangling role to the object owner. As far as I know that mapping is closer to what REASSIGN OWNED does on v17 and later, and it would match a fresh install.
objections.author_must_show: Why drop items with a dangling grantor or grantee instead of substituting the object owner, so upgraded extension members dump the same as a fresh install?

critic.reasoning: Messages #33 to #35 confirm the drift, and message #19 suggests keeping a grant whose grantor is dangling, so the design question stands. P3 concerns a pg_upgrade check and must not be used as support; the renamed-member restore failure is speculative.

objections.title: Filter runs on every dump, including from v17+ servers where it cannot match
objections.failure_scenario: Someone running HEAD pg_dump against a v19 server with many tables pays for the SAFE_INITPRIVS subquery in the per-table column ACL query on every table, although dangling rows cannot exist there. Years later, a developer changing the pg_init_privs queries cannot tell whether the macro is still needed. Nothing fails if the filter is dropped or missing from a new query site.
objections.argument: Message #4 and message #32 show dangling rows only come from pre-v17 servers, yet v6 to v9 apply the filter without a remoteVersion check. Message #23 objected to the per-table subquery, and Tom Lane, who raised the cost concern in message #14, gives no view on v6 or later. The only measurement, in message #26, used empty tables with no pg_init_privs rows and runs that varied between 19 and 25 minutes, so it does not exercise the new path. A version gate would limit both the cost and the scope of the code kept in HEAD.
objections.author_must_show: Why not apply SAFE_INITPRIVS only when the source server is older than v17, so HEAD dumps of modern servers skip the per-table subquery?

critic.reasoning: No visible patch version gates the filter on server version, although message #4 says v17 and later cannot have dangling rows. The cost part is likely overstated: as far as I know, pg_dump since v15 runs the column ACL query only for tables that have column ACLs.

refuted.title: Every dump pays a per-table subquery for a rare broken case
refuted.failure_scenario: A user runs pg_dump or pg_upgrade on a database with tens of thousands of tables and no dangling entries. The SAFE_INITPRIVS subquery still runs once per table in dumpTable(). They see a slower dump after a minor update and get nothing in return.
refuted.argument: Tom Lane in message #22 calls the affected group "vanishingly small", and Laurenz Albe in message #13 notes "very few reports". The thread shows one field report (message #1), and in message #32 the problem does not reproduce on current releases. Message #23 says the v6 per-table subquery brings back the cost Tom objected to in message #14. The only measurement, in message #26, varied between 19 and 25 minutes, so it cannot show a small per-table cost, and it did not time pg_dump on its own.
refuted.author_must_show: What is the pg_dump-only time, with and without the patch, on a database with many tables and column ACLs, measured with run-to-run variance well below the difference?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-1 on the per-table cost. On desirability, the patch fixes a failed pg_upgrade and follows the pg_dump direction Tom Lane suggested in message #4; P10 was an optimization patch and does not apply.

touch_points.label: on-disk format / pg_upgrade
touch_points.reason: The fix changes what pg_upgrade restores; affected extension members lose their pg_init_privs row in the new cluster.

touch_points.label: catalog changes
touch_points.reason: pg_dump changes how it reads pg_init_privs and checks role OIDs against pg_roles; no catalog definition changes.

touch_points.label: pg_dump / restore round-trip
touch_points.reason: pg_dump drops dangling aclitems, so later dumps of upgraded extension members re-emit REVOKE and GRANT lines.

touch_points.label: security / privileges
touch_points.reason: The patch decides which initial privileges survive a dump; it filters by OID against pg_roles to avoid a name-matching risk (messages #17, #18).

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: The author proposes a backpatch to v15, but the CF target is 19 and the range is not agreed.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The SAFE_INITPRIVS macro stays in two pg_dump query sites with no server version gate.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: The filter subquery is added to the per-table column ACL query in dumpTable().

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Why does the filter drop an aclitem whose grantor alone is dangling, such as =r/16449, instead of keeping the grant with the object owner as grantor?
Why is SAFE_INITPRIVS not applied only when the source server is older than v17, given that message #4 says later servers cannot have dangling rows?
What is the pg_dump-only time with and without the patch on a database with many tables that have column ACLs and pg_init_privs rows?
Which branches should get the fix, and does a test run pg_dump against a v15 or v16 source server that has dangling rows?
Does the pg_dump fix depend on the HEAD-only putid() quoting change, and has that patch been posted?

committability.owner_note: Needs a committer who knows pg_dump's ACL and pg_init_privs handling. Tom Lane raised the cost concern and the putid() idea, but shows no view on v6 to v9.
committability.liability: The owner signs for changed pg_dump output in back branches, for the loss of pg_init_privs rows on upgraded clusters, and for the filter staying in HEAD while pre-v17 source servers are supported.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted nine versions over about four months and returned the entry to Needs review after each rebase and review round.

priority.reason: The patch touches one pg_dump source file plus a test and fixes a hard pg_upgrade failure for clusters with extensions installed by later-dropped roles. Two reviewers report no open items, so the entry waits for a committer in this area to settle the two design points and the backpatch range.

provisional_note: Without the code, I could not check that the filter covers every query that reads pg_init_privs, nor how often the per-table column ACL query runs. The behaviour against v15 and v16 source servers is untested in the material.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Avoid race condition between "GRANT role" and "DROP ROLE"".
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Avoid race condition between "GRANT role" and "DROP ROLE"".
Reverted commit(s): Avoid race condition between "GRANT role" and "DROP ROLE".
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 98fc31d6499163a0a781aa6f13582a07f09cd7c6.
That change allowed DROP OWNED BY to drop grants of the target
role to other roles, arguing that nobody would need those
privileges anymore.  But that's not so: if you're not superuser,
you still need admin privilege on the target role so you can
drop it.

It's not clear whether or how the dependency-based approach
to solving the original problem can be adapted to keep these
grants.  Since v18 release is fast approaching, the sanest
thing to do seems to be to revert this patch for now.  The
race-condition problem is low severity and not worth taking
risks for.

I didn't force a catversion bump in 98fc31d64, so I won't do
so here either.

precedents_retrieved.title: pg_dump -C Grant statement on create database
precedents_retrieved.summary: When pg_dump is run with -C (emit CREATE DATABASE), it would also emit the database-level GRANT statements (such as GRANT CREATE ON DATABASE), matching what pg_dumpall already produces. The patch makes emitting these grants subject to the existing -x (no privileges) option.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The thread contains only the original report, a reply agreeing it is an oversight, and the patch submission; no review or objection to the patch appears, and the entry was returned with feedback about three months later.

precedents_retrieved.title: DROP PRIVILEGES OWNED
precedents_retrieved.summary: A new command, DROP PRIVILEGES OWNED BY role [, ...], removes all privileges granted to a role in the database while keeping the objects the role owns. The author noted that extending DROP OWNED to accept what to drop might be a better design than a separate command.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Heikki Linnakangas objected to the verb and proposed REVOKE syntax, such as REVOKE ALL PRIVILEGES FROM <role>, and the author agreed. No revised patch followed, and Michael Paquier marked the entry returned with feedback because the author had not responded for a few weeks.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
DROP seems like the wrong verb here. DROP is used for deleting objects,
while REVOKE is used for removing permissions from them.

precedents_retrieved.title: pg_dump: optimize dumpFunc()
precedents_retrieved.summary: Replace pg_dump's per-function query in dumpFunc() with a single query that gathers data for all functions up front, keeping the PGresult in memory and using a sorted array of function OIDs to locate each function's row. The aim was to reduce dump time for databases with many functions (shown as about 0.25s to about 0.11s for 10k simple functions).
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane questioned whether the change helps databases with few functions and what it does to pg_dump's memory requirements when there are very many functions with large source text, and said the shown results did not justify the risk. The author agreed and withdrew the patch.

I'm not sure that the results you're showing justify taking any
risk here.

precedents_retrieved.title: orphaned function
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes QualifiedNameGetCreationNamespace() take a lock on the target schema, so a concurrent DROP SCHEMA cannot leave a function without a namespace. A reviewer added a separate patch that also locks the function's argument types, return type and language.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane said the schema lock alone does not close the race and needs retry logic like RangeVarGetAndCheckCreationNamespace. He also asked why only this dependency should be covered, and pointed to a general approach based on pg_depend. The author agreed and proposed a different design that checks a catalog snapshot during DROP, but sent no patch. David Steele marked the entry Returned with Feedback because a new patch was needed and, after Alvaro Herrera's comment, the change looked like a new safety feature that could not be back-patched as a bug fix.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I don't think that actually succeeds in preventing the race, it'll just delay your process till the deletion is committed.

roaster_notes.note: The one close precedent, [P3], argued against the pg_upgrade pre-check that message #1 first proposed, and message #4 moved the work to pg_dump, so that reason does not apply to v9. Message #3 links an earlier thread on the pg_upgrade-check patch, and message #4 cites the role-GRANT fixes as the model, but the material does not record a rejection reason that would still apply.

From the standards and compatibility angle, the patch adds no syntax, GUC or psql change. The silent filtering matches what Tom Lane cites for role grants in message #4. The putid() quoting change would alter aclitem text for clients, but it is a separate HEAD-only proposal and not judged here.

The proposal changes only the SQL that pg_dump sends; it adds no WAL record, catalog column, on-disk format or protocol message. The one lasting effect, extension members losing their pg_init_privs row after upgrade, came up in message #33, was confirmed by a real upgrade in message #35 and is stated in the v9 commit message, so I do not raise it again.

No security objection remains for v9. The only privilege risk in the thread was a CREATEROLE user creating a role named after a dangling OID to receive its grants (message #17), and v6 removed it by filtering on OID against pg_roles (message #18). pg_roles is readable by any role, so non-superuser pg_dump gains no new visibility, and the filter only removes items for roles that no longer exist.

The fix itself fits core. It is a pg_dump-side repair of a real upgrade failure, a different approach from the pg_upgrade pre-check in [P3]. The putid() HEAD-only patch is separate and not judged here.

The only existing way is the workaround in message #1: delete pg_init_privs rows directly with allow_system_table_mods. Tom Lane (message #4) calls manual correction tedious and error-prone, and catalog surgery is not a documented idiom, so it does not meet the need. No contrib module or extension can repair pg_dump's own ACL output during pg_upgrade. The proposal follows the pg_dumpall precedent for dangling role grants, so it adds no second mechanism.

Demand is narrow but real. Failed upgrades from v15 and v16 clusters with extensions installed by later-dropped roles are a recorded bug, and Tom Lane proposed the pg_dump direction himself in message #4. The only demand-side concern is that all dump users pay for a fix that a few users need.
